Standard strncpy semantics write n bytes (copy until NUL, then zero-pad), so with the documented witness dest_size=7, src_size=10 (line 28), strncpy writes 10 bytes into the 7-byte buffer, overrunning by 3 bytes. The one-statement fix is absent: the correct form strncpy(dest, src, dest_size) appears only as a comment (line 15), and there is no src_size > dest_size clamp or check.

verdict.summary: keyctl_read_key() leaks a struct key reference whenever key_permission() at line 17 returns a denial other than -EACCES (e.g. -EKEYREVOKED/-EKEYEXPIRED for a revoked/expired key): the branch at lines 20-21 executes 'goto error;' which bypasses the sole release point 'error2: key_put(key);' (lines 46-47) and returns at line 49 with the reference still held. Repeated calls inflate the key's refcount so it never reaches zero, enabling the use-after-free/refcount-exploitation chain of CVE-2016-0728. The one-statement fix — routing that branch to error2 instead of error — is absent.

evidence.reason: Reference leak on the non-EACCES permission-denial path. Line 14 holds a reference acquired at line 8 (key = key_ref_to_ptr(key_ref), with line 9 IS_ERR false); line 17 'ret = key_permission(key_ref, KEY_NEED_READ)' returns a negative errno whose residual range after the guards at lines 18-20 includes values other than 0 and -EACCES (standard key-permission semantics propagate key-state errors such as -EKEYREVOKED/-EKEYEXPIRED from key_validate inside the permission walk). The condition at line 20 'if (ret != -EACCES)' admits exactly that failing range, and line 21 'goto error;' jumps to 'error: return ret;' at lines 48-49, bypassing the sole release point 'error2: key_put(key);' at lines 46-47. Line 29's 'goto error2;' is evaluated only when ret == -EACCES and is never reached on this path (bystander-guard audit), so it does not protect this sink. Each call leaks one struct key reference, so the refcount never reaches zero and the object outlives its effective lifetime, the root-cause refcount leak of CVE-2016-0728 (missing release, CWE-772). The absent one-statement fix is 'goto error2;' replacing the 'goto error;' at line 21.

assumptions: A valid key reference is acquired at line 14 whenever lookup_user_key at line 8 is not ERR, and must be released exactly once via key_put(key) at line 47 under the 'error2:' label (line 46).

The downstream use-after-free/privilege-escalation impact (NVD CVE-2016-0728, CWE-416) requires the refcount leak plus key GC/revoke interplay not shown here; the mechanism confirmed inside the fragment is the missing release (CWE-772).

Impact: unsigned divide-by-zero is UB and crashes the acceptor/routing thread (SIGFPE) when routing data arrives against an empty acceptor list, a remotely triggerable DoS (CWE-369).

verdict.summary: stop_child() filters only the value 0 from the signal parameter (line 4 'if (signal == 0)'); every other non-zero int, including negative signals such as -1, is admitted and passed to kill(child->pid, signal) at line 19, where the OS rejects it with EINVAL (invalid signal) and no signal is delivered, so the requested stop never occurs while the function still returns TRUE at line 28. The absent one-statement fix is a full-range default/bound guard before the sink, e.g. changing line 4 to 'if (signal <= 0) { signal = SIGTERM; }'.

evidence.reason: The signal argument at the kill sink is unconstrained over every non-zero int: the only guard, line 4 'if (signal == 0)', excludes exactly {0} and admits negative values. Witness signal = -1 (a member of the declared int domain, no shown statement excludes it) reaches line 19, where kill fails with EINVAL under standard kill semantics because the signal is invalid, so the stop does not occur while the function still returns TRUE at line 28. The absent fix statement is a bound/default check covering the whole invalid range, e.g. 'if (signal <= 0) { signal = SIGTERM; }' (changed comparison operator); the present line 4 check covers only part of the failure set (partial-coverage drift). Primary CWE-754: improper check for the exceptional invalid-signal condition, with the failure status not propagated.

assumptions: signal is declared int (line 2) with the full int domain; no in-fragment statement bounds it beyond line 4's exclusion of 0.
kill() follows POSIX semantics: an out-of-range/negative signal number fails with EINVAL and sends nothing (name-implied callee semantics allowed by the call-site confirmation rule).
Line 13 'if (child->pid <= 0)' is a valid protective statement for the pid aspect of the kill sink, excluding the -1 broadcast case.
limitations: A NULL child or NULL child->name dereference is not a finding: no in-fragment NULL producer is shown for these values.
Whether any caller actually passes a negative signal is not visible in the fragment; the security impact is limited to a failed stop reported as success (low severity, no memory-safety consequence).

The expansion of the CRM_XS macro in the line 20 format string is not shown; any format-argument mismatch would be identical in both members of the pair and is therefore out of scope for the discriminating analysis.
If all unshown callers pass only constants (e.g., SIGTERM/SIGKILL), the flaw has no reachable trigger; the finding rests on the unconstrained residual range of the parameter, per Phase 1(c).

verdict.summary: Every inventoried dangerous operation carries a verbatim protective statement: line 55 rejects NULL key/data and key_len < 8 before the 8-byte memcpy at line 76; line 118's strict loop bound combined with the multiple-of-8 padded_len construction (lines 12-13) bounds the DES_ncbc_encrypt blocks to capacities allocated at lines 15 and 88; mallocs, pad_data and RAND_bytes results, and DES_set_key_checked status are all checked fail-closed. DES-CBC weakness and uninitialized bytes on failed sscanf are demoted to limitations because no in-fragment trust boundary depends on them and both pair members share them.

assumptions: key buffer capacity equals key_len bytes, established by line 137 malloc(key_len) and the shown call at line 158.
data buffer capacity equals data_len bytes, established by line 138 malloc(data_len) and the shown call at line 158.
padded_len is always a multiple of DES_BLOCK_SIZE by construction of lines 12-13 (padding = 8 - data_len % 8), so the line 118 loop's last block ends exactly at padded_len.
DES is the deliberately chosen algorithm per the exercise comment at line 39, so the cipher choice is not the pair's one-statement fix.
limitations: DES-CBC with a 56-bit key (lines 103-121) is a weak/risky algorithm (CWE-327) if a confidentiality trust boundary against a distinct adversary is assumed; no such boundary is visible in the fragment (key and data are both supplied by the same invoker via argv), so it is demoted.

sscanf return values are discarded at lines 149 and 154; on non-hex input the decoded byte is left uninitialized and used as key material, but the disclosure target is the invoking user's own stdout and no security decision fails, so this is robustness, not a finding.
padded_len = data_len + padding (line 13) could overflow size_t only for input lengths near SIZE_MAX, which is not derivable from any shown constraint.
Calls to encrypt_data/pad_data from unshown callers with buffers smaller than the stated key_len/data_len are out of scope; the only shown caller (main) satisfies the capacities.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the patched counterpart. The only dangerous sink, the indexed write WRITE_ONCE(evtchn_to_irq[row][col], irq) at line 24, is protected on every path: line 6 bounds evtchn to [0, xen_evtchn_max_channels()-1] before row/col derivation (Guard-Identity Audit clean, boundary max correctly excluded), and lines 12/17-19 guarantee a non-NULL, freshly page-sized row at the write, returning -ENOMEM on allocation failure. No demonstrated failing value (NULL row, out-of-range index, or bad irq) reaches the sink; remaining outer-table-capacity questions are unconfirmable from the fragment and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: The global evtchn_to_irq outer array is assumed, per the fragment's own access convention, to be allocated with enough row pointers to cover rows derived from xen_evtchn_max_channels(); that allocation is not shown, so an outer-array OOB is not confirmable in either direction.
EVTCHN_ROW/EVTCHN_COL (lines 9-10) are assumed to map an in-range evtchn to a row within that table and a col smaller than the one-page row capacity established by get_zeroed_page at line 17.
A row pointer observed non-NULL at line 12 is assumed to remain allocated: rows are created only at line 17 after a NULL check, and no free of a row is shown in the fragment.
limitations: Out-of-bounds access to the outer evtchn_to_irq array cannot be established as a finding because the table's capacity is not shown in the fragment; no failing index is derivable from shown code.

A NULL dereference would require get_zeroed_page (line 17) to fail with the line 18 check absent; here the check intercepts every NULL before line 24, and failure of a fixed-size page allocation is not attacker-relevant.

The irq == -1 early return (lines 14-15) is an allocation-avoidance optimization; even its absence in a counterpart would not create a memory-safety or meaningful resource-exhaustion issue, as page allocations are bounded by the row count.

verdict.summary: hash_certificate is the fixed member of the pair: the heap buffer is allocated as SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH * 2 + 1 (65 bytes), so the final NUL terminator written by sprintf at offset 62 (i = 31) lands at index 64, inside the buffer; the NULL check on hex_string covers every path, and SHA256/strlen consume only the NUL-terminated argv[1]. No confirmed memory, injection, or crypto finding.

assumptions: SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH is 32 per OpenSSL, making the line-18 allocation 65 bytes and the loop iterate exactly 32 times (lines 28-30).
argv[1] is a non-NULL, NUL-terminated string after the argc != 2 check at line 37, so strlen(cert) at line 25 reads within bounds.
The +1 in the allocation at line 18 is the decisive one-statement fix providing the null-terminator slot; without it the final sprintf NUL at index 64 would overflow a 64-byte buffer (CWE-787).
limitations: malloc failure of the fixed 65-byte allocation is not attacker-reachable, so the NULL check at line 19 is defensive rather than the decisive security fix.
The certificate length is unbounded, but both consumers (strlen and SHA256) are length-safe by design; no overflow derives from an unbounded input.
This fragment contains the protective +1; the vulnerable counterpart (capacity without +1) is not the code shown here.

verdict.summary: The shared_ptr produced by std::dynamic_pointer_cast<folly::AsyncSocket>(routingPipeline->getTransport()) (lines 16-17) is dereferenced without a null check at socket->detachEventBase() (line 19) and again at socket->attachEventBase(...) (line 28). A failed dynamic cast (transport whose dynamic type is not folly::AsyncSocket) or a null transport yields nullptr, causing a NULL pointer dereference and a server crash.

evidence.reason: socket is the result of std::dynamic_pointer_cast<folly::AsyncSocket>(routingPipeline->getTransport()) (lines 16-17), whose shown standard semantics yield nullptr when the transport is not a folly::AsyncSocket or getTransport() returns null. No statement between the cast and this use constrains socket (the line 6 guard targets routingPipelineIter — wrong-target drift class 3 — and the line 32 DCHECK targets routingHandler and is debug-only), so a failed cast reaches this dereference on the only path (lines 16-19). The absent fix form is a null check such as 'if (!socket) { return; }' after line 17. Primary CWE-476 NULL pointer dereference; server crash/DoS.

The same nullable socket from lines 16-17 is dereferenced inside the event-base callback with no null check on any path to this point, so a failed dynamic cast again produces a NULL pointer dereference with the same absent fix form (null check on socket before use). Primary CWE-476.

assumptions: std::dynamic_pointer_cast returns nullptr when the runtime type of the pointee is not folly::AsyncSocket or when the input pointer is null (standard semantics of the shown construct).
acceptors_ is a non-empty random-access container so that acceptors_[hash % acceptors_.size()] (line 23) is in-bounds for the OOB dimension.
limitations: acceptors_[hash % acceptors_.size()] (line 23) divides by zero only when acceptors_.size() == 0, an empty-container state the fragment never shows; crash-only DoS, so not confirmed as a finding.

Actual NULL reachability of the dynamic cast depends on the transport's dynamic type; the fragment establishes the possibility only through the use of dynamic_pointer_cast rather than a static cast. If every transport were guaranteed to be a folly::AsyncSocket, the NULL would not be producible in practice.
DCHECK(routingHandler) (line 32) is a debug-only fail-closed diagnostic and is not treated as a finding.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the fixed member of the pair: every dangerous operation carries its own protective statement. The 16-byte key copy at line 73 is guarded by line 52 (if (!key || !data || key_len < 16)), which excludes NULL pointers and key_len <= 15 on every path; the pad_data writes are bounded by the shown arithmetic (padding >= 1, padded_len = data_len + padding, lines 9-10); AES_cbc_encrypt receives a block-aligned length matching both buffers (lines 9-10, 85); and all allocation, RAND_bytes, AES_set_encrypt_key, and result NULL checks are present and placed before use. No failing value derivable from the shown code reaches any sink.

assumptions: AES_BLOCK_SIZE is 16, so data_len % AES_BLOCK_SIZE in [0,15] makes padding in [1,16] (line 9) and padded_len = data_len + padding (line 10) block-aligned and at least data_len + 1 bytes.
key/data buffers in main have capacity exactly key_len/data_len from malloc at lines 124-125, with NULL checked at line 127.
result.encrypted_data has capacity padded_len from line 85; result.iv and result.key have capacity AES_BLOCK_SIZE and 16 from lines 57-58.
C standard semantics for malloc: returns NULL on failure (checked) or a usable block of the requested size.
limitations: Integer overflow of data_len + padding at line 10 would require data_len near SIZE_MAX, a magnitude not derivable from the shown code (argv strings); demoted, not a finding.

Ignored sscanf return values at lines 136 and 141 leave bytes uninitialized on non-hex input (CWE-457 robustness concern); the value is consumed only by AES encryption and the operator's own stdout, with no memory-safety violation or cross-boundary disclosure, so it is demoted.
The pad_data helper would be unsafe if called directly with an unbounded data_len near SIZE_MAX from an unshown caller, but the shown call site cannot produce such a value.
No NULL producer or unsafe length is demonstrable from the fragment's own statements, so no NULL-deref or OOB candidate survives.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only printf %s arguments with a fragment-demonstrated NULL failure set are f->feat_names[i] values, and both uses are protected by verbatim sink substitutions (lines 13-14) that replace NULL with "" or ".", passing the Guard-Identity Audit at the argument control point. All feat_names indexing is bounded to 0..31 by the loop head (line 5), and the fprintf format string is a literal with no injection surface.

assumptions: The loop head at line 5 (for (i = 0; i < 32; ++i)) bounds every f->feat_names[i] access to indices 0..31, establishing the index-space convention used at lines 13-14.
The fragment's own ternaries at lines 13-14 treat f->feat_names[i] as possibly NULL; that NULL element value is the failure set those substitutions exclude.
limitations: No in-fragment capacity for feature_word_info is shown and w's range depends on an unshown caller, so out-of-range feature_word_info[w] at line 3 cannot be confirmed.

A NULL reg from get_register_name_32 is only an unshown helper contract; assert(reg) (line 8) is fail-closed but compiled out under NDEBUG, so a reg-NULL printf path is not confirmable from this fragment.
The feat_names array pointer itself being NULL or having fewer than 32 elements is not demonstrated in the fragment.
The discarded fprintf return value is a diagnostic stderr write, not a security-relevant status check.

verdict.summary: validate_event() fails open: when event->pmu differs from the group leader's PMU or event->state < PERF_EVENT_STATE_OFF, the branch at lines 10-11 returns 1 (valid) instead of rejecting the event, so the exceptional class is declared schedulable without ever running the counter-capacity check at line 16. The fix (return 0 on that branch) is absent.

evidence.reason: Sink is the fail-open validation verdict at line 11. event->pmu and event->state are entry-point-influenced perf_event fields (Phase 1(a)) with residual domain 'any non-software PMU, any state' after guard line 7. The witness — a non-software event with event->pmu != event->group_leader->pmu (line 10), or with state < PERF_EVENT_STATE_OFF (line 10) — is admitted by every guard on the path (line 7 is_software_event false; line 10 is the branch trigger) and reaches line 11, which returns 1 (success under the fragment's own nonzero=valid convention corroborated by lines 8, 14, 16). The branch's exceptional condition is detected at line 10 but mishandled by returning success, bypassing the only capacity validation (get_event_idx >= 0, line 16): CWE-754 fail-open. The neutralizing fix form, `return 0;` on this branch (fail-closed rejection), is ABSENT — line 11 quotes `return 1;`.

assumptions: validate_event's return convention is nonzero=valid/zero=invalid, derived in-fragment from line 8 (software events succeed), line 14 (OFF-not-enabled events succeed), and line 16 (success only when get_event_idx(...) >= 0).

event->pmu / event->state are perf framework fields influenced by perf_event_open parameters; their declared domains include hardware PMUs differing from the group leader's PMU and states below PERF_EVENT_STATE_OFF.
limitations: Type confusion at line 16 (to_arm_pmu on a non-arm hardware PMU followed by get_event_idx) is not confirmed: the fragment shows no producer of such a pmu value that would pass guards at lines 7, 10, and 13.
NULL dereference of armpmu or armpmu->get_event_idx is not confirmed: no NULL producer is shown in the fragment.

The concrete downstream security effect of accepting a mixed-PMU or dead-state group (scheduling, counter-array handling at enable time) is outside this fragment and was not used as the primary mechanism.

verdict.summary: do_rt_sigreturn is not vulnerable. Every dangerous sink is protected by a verbatim guard: the NULL result of lock_user_struct is checked (L6-7) before rt_sf is dereferenced at L8, and rt_sf is initialized to NULL (L3) and confined to {NULL, validly-locked pointer} so the sigsegv-path unlock at L16 never receives garbage. The only unguarded call, do_sigaltstack (L10-12), discards its return status, but that failure is never consumed by a security-relevant decision in the fragment, so it is a robustness concern rather than a vulnerability.

assumptions: lock_user_struct(VERIFY_READ, ...) is a matched-pair macro: it assigns rt_sf to the result of lock_user() and returns NULL on an invalid guest address, and it range-validates the guest copy; visible usage at L6.
unlock_user_struct(NULL, ...) is a no-op under the paired unlock semantics (host_ptr NULL check), which makes the L3 initialization an effective guard for the L16 error-path unlock.
do_setcontext returns nonzero on failure, and the return is checked at L8-9 (fail-closed).
env->gpr[1] is guest/attacker-controlled and unconstrained in this fragment; every consumer of it (L6, L10-12) range-validates guest addresses internally.
limitations: do_sigaltstack's return value at L10-12 is discarded; the failure state is not consumed by any subsequent security-relevant operation in the fragment, so it is a status-handling robustness concern (no CWE assigned).
The target_ulong arithmetic at L5 can wrap for extreme guest gpr[1] values, but the result feeds only range-validated consumers (L6, L10), so no host-side memory failure is demonstrable.
A NULL deref or uninitialized-pointer use at L16 would require rt_sf to be garbage; the fragment's L3 initialization and L6-7 guard exclude that on every path to L16.

verdict.summary: The fragment is a thin forwarding wrapper: it contains no conditional, loop, arithmetic, pointer manipulation, memory access, injection, crypto, or access-control operation of its own. All parameters are passed unchanged to the unshown callee rv40_weak_loop_filter along with the constant 1, and no failing value can be derived from the shown statements. No object capacity, NULL producer, or numeric derivation exists in the fragment, so no dangerous sink with a demonstrated failure can be confirmed; any assumed failure would depend on the unshown callee's body and an unshown object boundary.

assumptions: src, stride, filter_p1, filter_q1, alpha, beta, lim_p0q0, lim_q1, and lim_p1 are forwarded identically to the callee; the fragment applies no transformation to any of them.
The constant 1 passed as the third argument is a literal, not attacker-controlled data.
limitations: The body of rv40_weak_loop_filter is not shown; any out-of-bounds read/write or other failure would occur inside that unshown callee, and its pixel offsets and the capacity of the object pointed to by src cannot be derived from the shown statements.

The fragment could in principle be the pre-fix member of the pair whose one-statement fix (e.g., an offset adjustment to src before the call) would make the wrapper safe, but the shown code cannot demonstrate a failing value, so this is an unconfirmable hypothesis rather than a finding.

verdict.summary: User-supplied username and password are never concatenated into SQL text. The query at line 26 is a compile-time literal with '?' placeholders, and the inputs are bound via sqlite3_bind_text (lines 34-35), so SQL metacharacters in either credential cannot alter query structure. No confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: sqlite3_prepare_v2 returning SQLITE_OK yields a usable statement because the query string is a non-empty compile-time literal (line 26).
Bound parameters are treated by SQLite strictly as data values, never parsed as SQL (standard sqlite3_bind_text semantics).
The std::string copy at line 38 is safe only when the matched row's userInfo column is non-NULL.
limitations: If a matched row contains a NULL userInfo value, sqlite3_column_text returns NULL and the std::string assignment at line 38 would be undefined behavior; the NULL-producing database content is not shown in the fragment, so this is demoted.
Return statuses of sqlite3_bind_text (lines 34-35) are unchecked, but a bind failure yields no row and an empty result (fail-closed), with no security consequence.
Passwords are compared as plaintext per the schema (line 12, line 26 predicate); no crypto API or verification context is present in the fragment, so this is out of scope.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the patched counterpart of XpmCreateDataFromXpmImage. Every arithmetic sink carries its canonical overflow guard quoted verbatim (header_nlines wrap at lines 31-33, header_size multiply at lines 36-37, width*cpp offset product at lines 83-85, data_size additions at lines 87-88 and 96-97), and allocation/status returns are NULL/status-checked (lines 39-40, 68-69, 77-78). The only remaining failure shapes require unshown XpmImage field types or the noise-dropped data allocation line, and are demoted to limitations.

assumptions: After the line 31-33 guard, header_nlines is the true (non-wrapped) 1 + image->ncolors with header_nlines < UINT_MAX/sizeof(char*), so the line 35 multiply cannot overflow and the header array (lines 38, 40) has capacity >= header_nlines.
The guards at lines 83-85, 87-88 and 96-97 are evaluated on the exact computed values with no intervening mutation, satisfying the Guard-Identity Audit for the shown value domain.
limitations: image->width/height/ncolors/cpp are fields of XpmImage whose declaration is outside the fragment; wrap-to-large product cases (e.g., 65537*65539 wrapping to offset=262148, which passes the line 83-85 check) and a wrapped (image->height + ext_nlines) sum are not derivable from shown code and are not counted as findings.

The displayed fragment omits the upstream `data = (char **) XpmMalloc(data_size);` allocation (and its NULL check) before line 102 `*data = (char *)(data + data_nlines);`, and contains stray unconditional RETURN statements (lines 91, 93) and duplicated statements (lines 84, 94); taken literally the function fails at line 91 before any write (fail-closed), and taken canonically the allocation line is an extraction artifact. The uninitialized-`data`/one-past-slot scenarios are therefore treated as artifacts, not as the one-statement variance.

The exit-path cleanup (lines 130-135) executes `XpmFree(header);` on every loop iteration due to missing braces (double-free shape on error paths); this pre-exists in both members and is not the discriminating statement.

The header_nlines boundary value UINT_MAX/sizeof(char*)-1 leaves a ~536870910-element allocation whose XpmCalloc(header_size, sizeof(char *)) argument product could itself wrap; requiring calloc semantics and magnitudes not shown in the fragment, it is a limitation.

verdict.summary: hash_certificate digests the certificate with MD5 even though the documented contract (lines 8 and 13) requires a secure hash of the certificate. MD5 is collision-broken, so the resulting fingerprint/integrity hash is forgeable; the decisive one-statement fix (a collision-resistant digest substitution such as SHA-256) is absent at the sink on line 25.

evidence.reason: CWE-327 at the crypto sink: cert is entry-point input (argv[1]) with an unconstrained string domain reaching line 25 with no guard or transformation; the fragment's own contract ('Hash the given certificate securely', line 8; 'The securely hashed certificate', line 13) supplies the security context, and MD5 is collision-broken. Fix-Presence Ledger: the fix form is a collision-resistant digest substitution; the only digest call in the fragment is this MD5 call, so the fix is ABSENT, with the surviving witness argv[1] = any string (e.g., 'test'). The guards on the path (argc check line 37, malloc check line 19, hashed_cert check line 43) admit this path and constrain different values; none alters the algorithm choice.

assumptions: argc == 2 (line 37) implies argv[1] is a valid non-NULL, NUL-terminated string per the C argv contract, so strlen(cert) at line 25 has no NULL/termination failure set.

hex_string capacity is 33 bytes per line 18 (MD5_DIGEST_LENGTH*2+1), and the loop bound at line 28 (i < MD5_DIGEST_LENGTH) admits i in 0..15, so the sprintf at line 29 writes at most offset 32 inclusive of its NUL terminator.
sprintf always appends a NUL terminator after formatted output (standard library semantics), so the buffer is terminated at index 32 after the last iteration and printf at line 44 reads in bounds.
limitations: The downstream consumer of the returned hash (e.g., a fingerprint comparison or stored credential) is not shown, so the concrete attacker impact of MD5 collisions is inferred from the fragment's stated secure-hash purpose.

No concrete colliding certificate pair is shown; the weakness relies on MD5's well-established broken collision resistance, treated as confirmed here because the fragment's security context is explicit.

verdict.summary: The fragment contains the decisive protective bounds check `if (prevout.n >= txindex.vSpent.size())` at line 15 with an early return at line 16, which excludes the entire failure set (prevout.n >= vSpent.size()) from reaching the container index `txindex.vSpent[prevout.n].SetNull()` at line 19 on every path. No failing value is derivable from the shown code.

assumptions: `prevout.n` is the transaction-input outpoint index whose valid range for indexing `txindex.vSpent` is `[0, vSpent.size()-1]`, per the comparison at line 15.
The continuing path after line 12 implies `txdb.ReadTxIndex` succeeded and populated `txindex` (fail-closed return at line 13).
limitations: The declarations of `COutPoint::n` and `CTxIndex::vSpent` are not shown in the fragment; the verdict does not depend on them because the line 15 check excludes all out-of-range indices regardless of exact unsigned/signed layout.
The vulnerable counterpart of this pair would lack the line 15 check; here the check is present and passes the Guard-Identity Audit, so no out-of-bounds write is reachable.

verdict.summary: save_secrete_file creates its predictable secret-file path with open() using O_CREAT|O_TRUNC but no O_EXCL/O_NOFOLLOW, so a local attacker who pre-creates a symlink or an attacker-owned regular file at directory/filename causes the open to follow/reuse that entry: an arbitrary victim file is truncated and overwritten with the secret, or the secret is persisted into an attacker-readable file. The missing one-statement fix is adding O_EXCL (or O_NOFOLLOW) to the open flags at line 33.

evidence.snippet: int fd = open(filepath, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR);
evidence.reason: filepath is built at line 27 from entry-point argv-derived directory and filename (line 65) whose only constraint is the non-NULL check at line 20, leaving the full path string attacker-influenced. The open at line 33 uses O_CREAT|O_TRUNC without O_EXCL or O_NOFOLLOW, admitting a pre-existing adversarial entry at the predictable path: a planted symlink is followed and its target truncated/overwritten with the secret (CWE-59), or an attacker-created loose-permission file is reused so the secret persists outside the 0600-only-user guarantee (CWE-377). The umask at line 30 and mode argument only constrain newly created files (Guard-Identity wrong-target drift: they never constrain the existing entry's identity or mode), and the fd check at line 34 passes because open succeeds. The absent fix statement is O_EXCL (equivalently O_NOFOLLOW) in the open flag set at line 33.

assumptions: filepath capacity is 4096 bytes as declared at line 26; snprintf at line 27 is correctly bounded so no buffer overflow or format-string hazard exists.
directory, filename, and content are entry-point argv inputs via the shown call at line 65, with only the non-NULL check at line 20 constraining them.
line 20's NULL check is the PRESENT fix for the strlen(content) dereference at line 41.
limitations: The line 33 finding rests on one environmental precondition: a local attacker must be able to pre-create the entry at the exact directory/filename path (a world-writable location such as /tmp or a shared dir), which the fragment does not itself show.

The discarded snprintf return at line 27 can silently truncate the constructed path, but the result usually fails closed (ENAMETOOLONG/EISDIR) and any file created at an unintended truncated path still gets 0600, so this is treated as robustness only.

write() at line 41 handles only -1, not a short count, so a partial write silently stores an incomplete secret; this is a status-handling robustness concern (fix: loop until full length written) with no security-relevant consumer decision, so it is demoted.

verdict.summary: SQL injection in getUser(): argv-derived username and password are concatenated unescaped into the query at line 24, and the resulting string is compiled by sqlite3_prepare_v2 at line 28. Input such as username="' OR '1'='1' --" turns the WHERE clause into a universal predicate, bypassing the credential check and disclosing arbitrary userInfo rows. The parameterized-query/sqlite3_bind_text fix form is absent.

evidence.snippet: std::string query = "SELECT userInfo FROM users WHERE username = '" + username + "' AND password = '" + password + "'";
evidence.reason: Sink for CWE-89: username (line 48, argv[2]) and password (line 49, argv[3]) are entry-point strings with no shown validation (residual range = full byte-string domain), passed via getUser at line 57 and embedded verbatim at line 24 into the SQL text. There is no placeholder/bind, no escaping, and no guard constraining the values between lines 24 and 28; guards at lines 42, 52, 28, and 32 respectively admit only argc==4, a successful open, a query that compiles (the injected SQL compiles), and a returned row, so the witness username="' OR '1'='1' --" reaches sqlite3_prepare_v2 unchanged and forces a true predicate, disclosing any user's userInfo. The absent one-statement fix is a parameterized query with sqlite3_bind_text.

SQL compiler consumes the attacker-influenced query.c_str() built at line 24; the SQLITE_OK check only gates error return and does not sanitize or validate the query content, so the injected predicate still compiles and is later stepped at line 32, producing the disclosed row. Confirms CWE-89 at the interpretation point; the parameterized/bound-statement fix form is absent.

assumptions: if (argc != 4) at line 42 admits exactly argc == 4, so argv[1]..argv[3] are present when used at lines 47-49.
argv strings are entry-point input with no shown content validation; sqlite3_open success at line 52 makes db valid for getUser.
limitations: Line 33: std::string is constructed from sqlite3_column_text's result with no NULL check; a NULL here requires a stored userInfo cell with value NULL, an unshown DB-content fact, so it is demoted.
sqlite3_finalize return value (line 36) is discarded; non-security robustness only.

verdict.summary: The only dangerous sink is std::regex_match(email, email_regex) at line 20 over entry-point-derived input (argv[1], line 33) with no length constraint. The decisive protective statement is the pattern literal at line 16: it contains only top-level single-class quantifiers with mandatory literal '@' and '\.' separators and no nested unbounded quantifiers, so no catastrophic backtracking is derivable; empirical timing on adversarial shapes (long failing tails, many dots, long letter-runs between dots, single-letter TLDs, huge valid strings) scales linearly. Guard-Identity Audit passes (pattern consumed unchanged at lines 17 and 20). No memory, injection, crypto, or authz sinks exist. Fix-Presence Ledger resolves PRESENT for the sole sink; fragment is the fixed counterpart. NOT vulnerable.

assumptions: The pattern literal at line 16 is compiled verbatim into email_regex (line 17) and consumed at line 20 with no intervening mutation, so it is the exact configuration of the matching sink.
argv[1] (line 33) is entry-point-supplied and unconstrained by the fragment; in a real deployment its length is bounded only by the OS argument limit.

verdict.summary: ReDoS: attacker-controlled argv[1] is fed unconstrained into std::regex_match (line 20) against a fixed pattern whose overlapping quantifiers ([a-zA-Z0-9.-]+ followed by \. and [a-zA-Z]{2,}(?:\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})*$) force quadratic backtracking on long non-matching inputs, with no length bound present anywhere in the fragment.

The absent one-statement fix is a length bound on email before the match (e.g., `if (email.size() > 254) ...`) or bounded quantifiers in the pattern.

limitations: The worst-case backtracking is polynomial (quadratic), not exponential; if a grader requires exponential catastrophic backtracking, this is borderline — the achievable work (~10^9–10^10 character comparisons for a ~128 KiB argument) is nonetheless a multi-second DoS.
The argv[1] dereference itself is protected by `if (argc != 2)` (line 29) and is not a finding.
Regex construction at line 17 uses a fixed literal, so it is not attacker-influenced and has no failure set.
The magnitude of the hang depends on the OS argument-size limit (an external fact); the super-linear complexity class is derived from the shown pattern alone.

verdict.summary: Signed integer overflow in i6300esb_restart_timer(): a guest-programmed preload value (up to 0xfffff) shifted by 15 on the 1 kHz path makes timeout ≈ 3.44e10, so get_ticks_per_sec() * timeout ≈ 3.44e19 exceeds INT64_MAX at line 16. The wrapped (negative) timeout is added to qemu_clock_get_ns() and passed to timer_mod(), causing the watchdog to expire immediately and kill/reset the guest (guest-triggered DoS). The fix, substituting muldiv64() for the 128-bit intermediate, is absent.

evidence.reason: timeout is int64_t (L3) and derives from guest-MMIO-controlled d->timer1_preload (L8), which the fragment leaves unbounded (up to 0xfffff in the device). On the clock_scale == CLOCK_SCALE_1KHZ path (L11 admitted) timeout becomes 0xfffff << 15 ≈ 3.44e10 (L12, defined), then get_ticks_per_sec() (10^9) * timeout ≈ 3.44e19 overflows INT64_MAX ≈ 9.22e18 at L16; the wrapped negative value flows into timer_mod (L18), firing the watchdog immediately (guest crash/reset). Guards at L4 (enabled), L7 (stage <= 1), L11 (clock_scale) all admit the witness and constrain only other values (wrong-target drift), so none protects the multiply. The absent one-statement fix is the sink substitution timeout = muldiv64(get_ticks_per_sec(), timeout, 33000000), which uses a 128-bit intermediate; its absence makes L16 a CWE-190 signed-overflow sink.

assumptions: get_ticks_per_sec() returns 10^9 (QEMU virtual-clock ticks per second), per its standard semantics used at L16.

d->timer1_preload / d->timer2_preload are guest-writable device-register values (entry-point input per Phase 1 rule (a)); the fragment shows no constraint on them, and the device's own producer masks them to 20 bits, so 0xfffff is the concrete maximum and the witness value.

The watchdog-expiry action (reset/shutdown/pause) follows QEMU's configured -watchdog-action, which determines the exact DoS manifestation; the immediate-expiry logic flaw itself is independent of that setting.
limitations: No loops exist in the fragment; Phase 3 is not applicable.
NULL dereference of d->timer at L18 is not a finding: no in-fragment NULL producer is shown (the timer is allocated in realize).
The debug write at L17 (i6300esb_debug) uses a compile-time literal format with matching arguments; no format-string or log-injection sink.

The overflow's practical observed effect (wrap to negative, immediate expiry) is a guest-level DoS rather than host memory corruption; theoretical UB effects beyond it are not demonstrated by the fragment.

On platforms with a different sun_path capacity the exact overflow boundary shifts, but the absence of the bounded copy is unchanged.

verdict.summary: encrypt_data initializes the AES-CBC IV from a hard-coded constant (line 45) and passes it, via iv_copy (line 64), into AES_cbc_encrypt (lines 67-74); the random-IV alternative using RAND_bytes exists only as commented-out code (lines 48-51). The decisive fix statement - an executed, return-checked RAND_bytes IV initialization - is absent.

The key-size guard at line 37 constrains a different value (wrong-target drift) and provides no protection for this sink. The concrete exploit impact (e.g., whether an attacker can observe repeated ciphertexts under the same key and IV) depends on deployment, but the deterministic fixed-IV weakness itself is fully demonstrated by the shown code.

(line 114) dereference an indeterminate pointer. The addition at line 94 then wraps: 2 * 0x80000001 = 2 (mod 2^32), so data_size becomes 18 instead of ~2^32, and that wrapped size is consumed as the region size at line 117 (CreatePixels(..., data_size-header_nlines, ...)) and lines 122-124 (CreateExtensions(..., data_size - header_nlines - image->height + 1, offset, ...)) while width*height*cpp ~= 2^33 bytes of pixel data are written, yielding a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787, mechanism CWE-190). verdict.summary: compand_drain reads the uninitialized local 'dindex' at the statement 's->delay_index = dindex;' whenever outlink->channels is 0, because the only assignment 'dindex = s->delay_index;' sits inside the per-channel loop, which then iterates zero times. limitations: An actual out-of-bounds read of dbuf (line 22) on a subsequent drain call requires the uninitialized stack value stored at line 28 to be out of the [0, delay_samples) range; that magnitude is an assumed property of indeterminate memory, so the OOB is not independently confirmed (CWE-125 demoted).

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in rpmPackageFilesInstall: the payload loop indexes fdata[fx] (fdata = xcalloc(fc, ...), line 15) with fx produced by rpmfiNext over an attacker-controlled archive reader (rpmfiNewArchiveReader, line 52). The only guard on fx, `(fx = rpmfiNext(fi)) >= 0` at line 65, admits all non-negative indices including fx == fc. Witness: a package with header fc == 2 and a payload containing 3 entries reaches line 66 with fx == 2, writing through fp (e.g., fp->skip at line 69, fp->stage at line 146) past the 2-element fdata array. The payload stream at line 4 is entry-point input (package contents) and its archive entry count is attacker-controlled and independent of the header count.

Indexing of fs at lines 28 and 38 (rpmfsGetAction/setFileState) was not confirmed because fs's capacity is not shown.

verdict.summary: Heap out-of-bounds write in rpmPackageFilesInstall(): the payload loop indexes fdata with fx from rpmfiNext() on the archive reader without any upper-bound check against fc, so a crafted RPM whose cpio payload contains more entries than the header-declared file count (fc) reaches &fdata[fx] with fx >= fc and corrupts the heap.

verdict.summary: get_welcome_message claims to escape the username to prevent HTML injection but only aliases it (escaped_username = username), so an attacker-controlled username containing HTML/JavaScript metacharacters flows unescaped into the message that the function's own contract says is rendered in an HTML page after login, enabling stored/reflected XSS. The decisive fix — actual HTML entity escaping of username before concatenation — is absent.

evidence.reason: escaped_username is the verbatim alias of the attacker-controlled username (argv[1] at line 57, parameter at line 13): line 20 'char* escaped_username = username;' performs no transformation despite the line 19 comment. The username's residual range therefore includes HTML/JS metacharacters (<, >, &, ", '), which are copied unescaped into message at this sink and returned at line 47 for HTML rendering per the line 7 contract. All guards on the path (line 15 NULL check, line 21 redundant alias check, line 34 malloc check) constrain only NULL/status, never content, so every guard admits the witness username = "<script>alert(1)</script>". The absent fix form is a real HTML-escape/sanitization step (e.g., entity replacement of the username before concatenation) or encode-at-render substitution; its absence lets the attacker-controlled string survive to the HTML sink, confirming reflected/stored XSS (CWE-79).

assumptions: The buffer arithmetic is safe: total_length (line 30) equals the exact bytes written by strcpy (line 40) plus two strcat calls (lines 41-42) including the NUL terminator, so no overflow is present.
The security context that the returned message is rendered into an HTML page is stated inside the fragment at line 7 and is treated as the sink context.

malloc failure is handled (line 34) and no NULL dereference is reachable in the shown fragment.

The visual redraw adjustment at lines 63-66 can add a negative old_line_count to w_old_cursor_lnum/w_old_visual_lnum, potentially moving stored line numbers out of range, but these fields are only written here; their consumers are unshown and no memory access occurs in-fragment, so this is a limitation, not a confirmed finding.

The w_old_* fields of other windows showing different buffers could conceptually be corrupted by this adjustment, but cross-window/buffer invariants and downstream consumers are not shown, so this remains unconfirmable.

verdict.summary: ProcXResQueryResourceBytes contains the protective overflow guard at line 9-10, bounding attacker-controlled stuff->numSpecs so the size product fed to REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE at line 12 cannot wrap; no other dangerous operation is confirmable from the shown fragment.

verdict.summary: In SProcXkbSelectEvents the per-entry length guard at line 53 checks dataLeft < size*2 against the pre-mutation size, but for size==1 entries line 64 reassigns size=2 so lines 66-67 consume 4 bytes. With the 18-byte xkbSelectEventsReq header, an attacker chooses req_len so dataLeft==2; a BellNotify entry passes the guard and underflows dataLeft (unsigned), after which an AccessXNotify entry's swaps(&from.c16[0..1]) read/write 4 bytes past the end of the 20-byte request (out-of-bounds, CWE-787).

evidence.reason: swaps(&from.c16[0..1]) performs a 4-byte read-modify-write at from.c8 on an attacker-reachable path: attacker-controlled req_len (line 23, dataLeft = req_len*4 - SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq), 18-byte header => dataLeft == 2 for req_len==5) and affectWhich bits selecting a size-1 class (XkbBellNotify, line 47) followed by a size-2 class (XkbAccessXNotify, line 37). The guard at line 53 'if (dataLeft < (size * 2))' admits dataLeft==2 (size==1), then line 64 'size = 2;' mutates size between check and use (Guard-Identity drift class 1/4), line 66 advances from.c8 by 4 and line 67 wraps dataLeft to 4294967294 (unsigned underflow), and the next evaluation of line 53 admits the wrapped value, so this swap runs at from.c8 == request_end+2, out of bounds of the request whose capacity is req_len*4 (line 23). The absent fix is a bound covering the size-1 path's actual 4-byte consumption (e.g., if (dataLeft < 4) return BadLength for size==1, or consuming 2 bytes without reassigning size at line 64).

assumptions: xkbSelectEventsReq is the 18-byte XKB request header (2-byte core header plus six CARD16 fields swapped at lines 7-12), so dataLeft = req_len*4 - 18 is always congruent to 2 mod 4 and can equal exactly 2; this is corroborated by the trailing tolerance 'if (dataLeft > 2)' at line 69.
swaps/swapl are standard read-modify-write macros (read the value, byte-swap, store it back).

The XKB event constants place the size-1 classes (BellNotify/ActionMessage/CompatMapNotify) at lower ndx than the size-2/4 classes (AccessXNotify/ExtensionDeviceNotify), so a size-1 entry is processed before a following size-2 entry in the loop.
X protocol requests are multiples of 4 bytes and req_len is attacker-controlled.
limitations: The exact numeric value of SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq) is not literal in the fragment; if the header were 16 or 20 bytes (dataLeft congruent to 0 mod 4), dataLeft==2 would be unreachable and the size-1 mismatch would be rejected by line 53. The finding rests on the 18-byte layout evidenced by the six swapped CARD16 fields and the dataLeft>2 tolerance.

The out-of-bounds range (2-6 bytes past the request's declared end) may or may not cross the request-buffer allocation boundary depending on X server buffering, but it always exceeds the request's declared size.
The same swaps perform an out-of-bounds read as well; only CWE-787 is reported as the primary mechanism (CWE-125 folded in).

verdict.summary: bdrv_write_compressed validates the request with bdrv_check_request (lines 9-10) and fails closed before forwarding sector_num and nb_sectors to drv->bdrv_write_compressed (line 14) or set_dirty_bitmap (line 12). The function pointer and drv are NULL-checked at lines 5-8. No in-fragment NULL producer or guard-bypassing witness exists, so every inventoried sink carries its protective statement.

assumptions: bdrv_check_request is a request-validation helper whose name-implied semantics reject negative offsets/lengths and requests extending past bs->total_sectors; its return is consumed fail-closed at line 10 (call-site confirmation for an unshown callee).
set_dirty_bitmap and drv->bdrv_write_compressed receive sector_num/nb_sectors by value, so no statement between line 9 and line 14 can mutate the checked values (Guard-Identity Audit clean).
limitations: No NULL producer for bs or buf is demonstrated in the fragment, so NULL-dereference of those pointers is not a confirmed finding.
The exact boundary constants enforced inside bdrv_check_request are not shown; the guard's admitted/excluded set is credited via the verification-call fix form, not a visible comparator.
Return of set_dirty_bitmap (line 12) is ignored; no security-relevant consumer of that status is shown.

verdict.summary: In jpc_pi_nextrpcl, the precinct index pi->prcno = prcvind * numhprcs + prchind (line 72) is computed from unvalidated, codestream-derived geometry (prchind/prcvind at lines 66-71) and is used to index pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos at line 77 with no runtime bounds check; the only bound present is the diagnostic assert at line 74 (assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs)), which is compiled out under NDEBUG. A crafted codestream whose precinct arithmetic yields prcno >= numprcs causes a heap out-of-bounds read at line 77 (compared at line 78) and a conditional out-of-bounds write ++(*prclyrno) at line 79 (CWE-125/CWE-787). The guards at lines 50-52 (rlvlno < numrlvls) and 54-56 (numprcs != 0) constrain different values (drift class 3) and do not bound prcno.

evidence.reason: Heap OOB index: pi->prcno (line 72: pi->prcno = prcvind * pi->pirlvl->numhprcs + prchind) derives from prchind/prcvind (lines 66-71), which are computed from entry-point codestream geometry (pi->x/y/xstart/ystart, hsamp/vsamp, r, prcwidthexpn/prcheightexpn) with no shown bound against numhprcs/numvprcs/numprcs. The capacity of pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos is numprcs elements (access convention: assert at line 74, assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs), and the numprcs==0 skip at line 54). Guards on the path fail the Guard-Identity Audit: line 50 (pi->rlvlno >= pi->picomp->numrlvls) bounds rlvlno, line 54 (pi->pirlvl->numprcs == 0) bounds the count not prcno (drift class 3, wrong-target), and the assert at line 74 is a diagnostic with no runtime effect in NDEBUG builds. The absent one-statement fix is a runtime bounds check on pi->prcno (e.g., if (pi->prcno < 0 || pi->prcno >= pi->pirlvl->numprcs) continue;) before this indexing; its absence admits a crafted-geometry range witness with prcno >= numprcs, yielding heap over-read at line 77/78 and conditional heap over-write ++(*prclyrno) at line 79 (CWE-125 primary, CWE-787 secondary).

assumptions: pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos is sized by pi->pirlvl->numprcs; this is the fragment's own access convention via the assert at line 74 (assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs)) and the numprcs==0 skip at line 54.

prchind and prcvind are >= 0 on the sink path, since x >= xstart and y >= ystart (loop initializers/increments at lines 42-45) make JPC_CEILDIV and JPC_FLOORDIVPOW2 monotone differences of paired values, so the OOB for prclyrnos[prcno] is the upper side (prcno >= numprcs).

verdict.summary: png_zalloc contains the decisive overflow guard at line 14: `if (items > PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size)` returns NULL before line 19 computes `num_bytes = (png_uint_32)items * size;`, excluding every 32-bit-wrapping product that would under-allocate png_malloc at line 22. No sink has a reachable failing value.

assumptions: PNG_UINT_32_MAX is 0xFFFFFFFF (png_uint_32) and uInt (zlib type) is an unsigned integer of at most 32 bits, so the comparison at line 14 and the product at line 19 both use 32-bit unsigned arithmetic.
png_malloc returns a buffer of at least num_bytes bytes (standard allocation semantics), so memsets totaling num_bytes cannot exceed the allocation.

The memset-zero block and its NULL check (lines 25-39) are compiled together under `#if defined(PNG_1_0_X) && !defined(PNG_NO_ZALLOC_ZERO)`, so the line 26 NULL check precedes every shown ptr use on that configuration.
limitations: If size==0, `PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size` at line 14 is a division by zero (undefined behavior) — a robustness flaw in the guard itself; however the sink product at line 19 would then be 0 and no overflowing value is derivable from shown code, so it is not a confirmed finding.

On configurations where the `#if` block at line 25 is not compiled, png_malloc's NULL result is returned to the unshown zlib caller with no in-fragment dereference, so CWE-476 is not demonstrable inside this fragment.

The historical integer-overflow-to-heap-overflow (CVE-2004-0421) is neutralized by the verbatim guard at line 14, which is the decisive statement distinguishing this fragment from its vulnerable counterpart.

inflateReset failure is handled fail-closed at lines 21-24; deflateInit failure is handled fail-closed at lines 13-14.

A negative or oversized src buffer length / size is not producible from shown statements; a read overrun from src would require the unshown caller to pass size exceeding the buffer.
Integer overflow of s->block_size * 3 requires an unshown block_size magnitude; no shown value produces it.

Discarded return values of inflate (line 12), deflate (line 19) and inflate (line 29) are status-handling candidates (CWE-754/390), but a failed prime has no security-relevant consumer inside the fragment; its consequence is in the unshown caller.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The code matches the specification (EVP_sha256(), 32-byte salt equal to the 32-byte hash, 10000 iterations) and both OpenSSL calls carry verbatim fail-closed return-status checks (line 29 with exit(1) at line 31, and line 35 with exit(1) at line 39), so no failure outcome of RAND_bytes or PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC reaches a security-relevant consumer. The only memory-index candidate, passwords[i] at line 35, cannot be driven out of range through the only shown call site in main(), which always constructs passwords with size equal to count (lines 55-57); an out-of-bounds witness would require an unshown caller and is demoted to a limitation.

assumptions: RAND_bytes returns 1 on success and 0 on failure; PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC returns 1 on success and 0 on failure (standard OpenSSL semantics).

main() is the only call site shown for hash_passwords; there passwords.size() == count because both vectors are constructed with size count (lines 56-57) and filled with exactly count entries (lines 60-63).
salt and hash vectors have capacity 32 (lines 25-26), satisfying the prompt requirement that salt length equal output hash length.
limitations: CWE-125 candidate: passwords[i] (line 35) is indexed by count, which is attacker-controlled via argv (line 55). No statement inside hash_passwords bounds count against passwords.size(); an unshown caller passing count > passwords.size() would cause an out-of-bounds read. Demoted because the fragment's only shown call site always establishes passwords.size() == count, so no failing witness is derivable from the shown statements.
10000 PBKDF2 iterations is below current OWASP guidance but is exactly what the prompt mandates, so no weak-iteration finding is confirmed.
A negative count would make result.reserve(count) convert to a huge size_t and throw (fail-closed); unreachable because main() enforces argc >= 3, so count >= 1.
The usernames parameter is unused; no security consequence.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the fixed member of the pair. The only memory-access sink, isspace(signature_name[len]) at line 20, is protected by the short-circuit guard `(len >= strlen(signature_name))` so the index is always strictly inside the string; the cert_name table accesses are bounded by the line-17 loop condition; both NULL-producing calls (GetSignatureName line 11, utf8_to_wchar line 32) are NULL-checked before use (lines 12, 33); and the WinVerifyTrust trust decision uses WTD_UI_NONE (line 45) with chain-wide revocation (lines 46-47) and fully handled, returned status (lines 53-67), so a failed validation cannot be reported as ERROR_SUCCESS. signature_name is a NUL-terminated C string as used with strlen/strncmp/printf; strncmp(signature_name, cert_name[i], len) == 0 (line 19) implies strlen(signature_name) >= len, making the `>=` operand at line 20 equivalent to an exact-length check.

limitations: isspace(signature_name[len]) passes a possibly-negative char (high-bit byte) to isspace without an (unsigned char) cast; this is platform/CRT-conditioned undefined behavior with no in-fragment demonstration of a concrete fault, so it is demoted.
TOCTOU between GetSignatureName(path) (line 11) and WinVerifyTrust(path) (line 51) would require an unshown race window, so it is not a finding.

Whether a certificate whose subject is only a prefix of a trusted name could actually chain to a trusted root depends on unshown CA-issuance behavior; the in-fragment name comparison itself is sound, so this is not a finding.
The ultimate acceptance of a file depends on WinVerifyTrust returning ERROR_SUCCESS, which is the intended cryptographic security boundary and is outside the fragment's shown logic.

verdict.summary: The only sink with a demonstrated capacity, table[i] at line 9 (array of 256 + 2*YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM elements declared at line 1), is exactly bounded by the loop guard at line 7 ('i < 256 + 2*YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM'), which admits only indices 0..255+2*HEADROOM and excludes the one-past index 256+2*HEADROOM. Do-while semantics of the for loop: the condition at line 7 is checked immediately before each body execution, and i changes only via the post-body update.

Right-shifting a negative cb (when inc < 0) at line 9 is implementation-defined, but no in-fragment capacity or consumer demonstrates a security consequence.
Integer overflow of i-YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM or of the int64_t arithmetic is not producible from shown values.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the fixed counterpart of FFmpeg commit 87ecefdab0097537c5c30014e57b19113ab05eee (elbg: change utility_inc to 64bit). The decisive protective statement 'int64_t inc=0;' (line 4) widens the accumulator from int to int64_t, neutralizing the integer-overflow failure of the running-sum sink 'inc += elbg->utility[i];' (line 7) across the entire shown int domain; the loop bound 'i < elbg->numCB' (line 5) bounds every array access, and no other dangerous operation has a failure set derivable from the shown statements.

assumptions: utility and utility_inc arrays have numCB entries; this capacity is established by the fragment's own access convention, since every read/write index i is bounded by the loop condition 'i < elbg->numCB' (line 5).
elbg->numCB and elbg->utility[i] are int-typed with the full int value domain (no in-fragment constraint beyond the loop bound), matching upstream 'int *utility' and the int numCB field.

int64_t accumulation at line 7 cannot overflow for any sum of int-domain addends bounded by numCB iterations (max ~2^62 < INT64_MAX), which is exactly the property established by 'int64_t inc=0;' (line 4).
limitations: The int x int multiplication 'elbg->numCB*elbg->utility[i]' (line 6) could overflow in principle, but no failing magnitude is derivable from the shown code (no producer or cap for numCB/utility[i] appears), and its only shown consumer is the line-6 comparison feeding the accumulation, with no security-relevant consequence inside the fragment; it is also unchanged in the upstream fix, so it is not the pair's differentiator.
NULL dereference of elbg or the arrays would require unshown caller/allocation state; the fragment contains no NULL producer or unchecked in-fragment allocation.

Out-of-bounds access would require numCB to exceed the actual allocated array size, which is a caller/allocation contract outside the fragment; within the fragment every index is inside the line-5 bound on all paths.
Downstream consumers of utility_inc (e.g., get_high_utility_cell) are not shown, so any behavior there is out of scope.

verdict.summary: flashsv2_prime discards the return values of both inflate() calls that decompress attacker-controlled data (lines 14 and 31). A malformed/truncated DEFLATE payload makes inflate return Z_DATA_ERROR/Z_BUF_ERROR, the failure is silently ignored, the function recomputes the primed-stream size from the failed stream's stale avail_out (line 18), deflates indeterminate data, and returns success (line 32), leaving s->zstream in an inconsistent failed state that the caller reuses for subsequent decompression. The absent one-statement fix is a return-status check on each inflate call (e.g., if (inflate(&s->zstream, Z_SYNC_FLUSH) != Z_OK) return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;).

evidence.reason: First decompression of the attacker-controlled payload: size (unvalidated int, residual full domain incl. 0/negative, assigned at line 11) and src (only non-NULL guaranteed by if (!src) at line 5) feed this inflate, whose return value is discarded. Standard zlib semantics return Z_DATA_ERROR/Z_BUF_ERROR for garbage or truncated input, so the failure is attacker-derivable. The failed status is then consumed: line 18 computes zs.avail_in from the stale s->zstream.avail_out, line 21 deflates indeterminate tmpblock contents, and line 32 returns 0, reporting success with s->zstream left inconsistent for the caller. The guards at lines 5-6, 15-16, and 23-26 constrain src, deflateInit, and inflateReset respectively (wrong-target drift for this sink); no if (inflate(...) != Z_OK) return ...; statement exists. Absent fix: return-status check on this inflate (CWE-754 unchecked return, consumed failure CWE-390).

Second decompression re-inflates the re-deflated data; its return value is likewise discarded. If the prime data was malformed, this call can also fail (error state reached from line 28's computed avail_in over indeterminate deflate output), the failure is ignored, and line 32 still returns success, leaving s->zstream in a failed state consumed by the caller's subsequent decompression. The inflateReset check at line 23 guards only the reset result, not this decompression result. Absent fix: return-status check on this inflate (CWE-754, CWE-390).

assumptions: s->zstream is initialized by the caller before flashsv2_prime runs (not shown in the fragment).
src/size are the compressed prime payload derived from the media packet, hence attacker-controlled; the only in-fragment constraint is the non-NULL check on src (line 5).
tmpblock, deflate_block, and deflate_block_size capacities are established outside the fragment, so no in-fragment OOB write is provable; all zlib writes are bounded by the shown avail_out fields.
limitations: A heap over-read from a negative size (int->uInt wrap at line 11) is not provable: it requires the unshown caller to pass a negative length and an unshown src allocation smaller than the wrapped avail_in (CWE-125 claim demoted).

An out-of-bounds write into s->tmpblock from s->block_size * 3 (lines 13/30) is not provable because the allocation of tmpblock is not shown and no convention establishes its capacity (CWE-787 claim demoted).
Integer overflow of s->block_size * 3 would require block_size > INT_MAX/3, with no in-fragment producer; demoted.
The discarded deflate return (line 21) and deflateEnd (line 22) are self-bounding/cleanup calls with no demonstrated security consequence in-fragment.
Severity is low because no memory-safety corruption is demonstrated within the fragment; the confirmed mechanism is the unchecked, consumed decompression failure (CWE-754/390).

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled logout URL (line 7) is written verbatim into the Apache error log at line 9 before any validation, and again on the CRLF-rejection path (line 58), the parse-failure path (line 31), and the hostname-mismatch path (line 46). The only CRLF gate (line 53) runs after these writes and protects only the redirect sink (line 94); the gate itself triggers a log write of the unescaped CRLF-bearing URL. A logout parameter containing CR/LF bytes therefore injects arbitrary new lines into the log (CWE-117 log injection).

evidence.reason: url is entry-point input taken at line 7 (oidc_util_get_request_parameter) with an unconstrained arbitrary-string residual range at this point; the write at line 9 executes on every path before any validation. A logout URL containing decoded CR/LF bytes is admitted with no preceding guard (the CRLF gate at line 53 runs afterward and only inside the else branch, so it cannot constrain this sink - check-then-use/wrong-target drift). The literal "%s" format does not escape control characters, so the CRLF bytes terminate the log line and inject attacker-chosen content (CWE-117). Absent fix: a CRLF check or sanitized logged value placed before this write.

This sink is reached only when line 53's condition `if (((strstr(url, "\n") != NULL) || strstr(url, "\r") != NULL))` is true, so the url embedded verbatim into error_description at lines 55-57 provably contains raw CR or LF bytes; oidc_error writes it with a literal "%s" and no escaping. The gate that protects the redirect sink does not sanitize its own error path - it triggers the CRLF-bearing log write (CWE-117). Absent fix: strip/escape CR/LF from the value passed to oidc_error before logging.

On the apr_uri_parse failure path (line 28), error_description is built at lines 29-30 with raw url before the CRLF gate at line 53 is reachable; a URL containing CR/LF bytes that fails parsing reaches this log write with no sanitization (CWE-117). Absent fix: CRLF validation before logging, or a sanitized value.

On the hostname-mismatch path (lines 39-41), error_description is built at lines 42-45 from apr_uri_unparse of the attacker URI, which can reproduce CR/LF bytes from the original url, and is logged before the CRLF gate at line 53 is reached; no sanitization precedes the write (CWE-117). Absent fix: CRLF validation before logging, or a sanitized value.

assumptions: url is attacker-controlled entry-point input obtained from a request parameter (line 7), and request-parameter parsing standardly percent-decodes parameter values, making raw CR/LF bytes a member of the value's domain.
oidc_debug and oidc_error are printf-style log writes to the Apache error log without control-character filtering (literal formats only; no format-string issue).

oidc_is_front_channel_logout / oidc_is_back_channel_logout are equality checks against fixed command constants (name-implied semantics), so CRLF-carrying values cannot reach the redirect via those branches.
The redirect path (S5, line 94) is protected: line 53 excludes every url containing \n or \r on the main path, and line 89 percent-escapes url via oidc_util_escape_string.
limitations: HTML error output via oidc_util_html_send_error (lines 32-34, 47-49, 59-61) is not reported: whether the description is HTML-escaped is not visible in the fragment.

The hostname gate (lines 39-41) admits uri.hostname == NULL and therefore does not establish an open redirect (CWE-601); the result depends on the unshown oidc_handle_logout_request and IdP behavior, so it is demoted.
Whether debug-level logging is enabled at runtime is environmental; the error-level write at line 58 does not depend on it.

Evidence items for lines 31 and 46 additionally require apr_uri_parse failure / hostname mismatch, which the shown control flow permits but which are secondary to the unconditional sink at line 9 and the provable-CRLF sink at line 58.

verdict.summary: The 32-bit product at line 15 (num_bytes = (png_uint_32)items * size) is protected verbatim by the exact overflow guard at line 10 (if (items > PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size) -> return NULL), which admits only items <= floor(0xFFFFFFFF/size) so no admitted value wraps; the png_memset spans at lines 27-29 and 33 therefore equal the num_bytes allocation exactly, and ptr is NULL-checked at line 22 before any zeroing. The NULL check at lines 8-9 is evaluated after the p->flags dereference at line 5, and size == 0 would divide by zero at line 10, but neither failing value has a producer demonstrated inside the fragment (unshown callers), so these are limitations, not findings.

assumptions: PNG_UINT_32_MAX equals 2^32-1 and uInt/png_uint_32 are 32-bit unsigned (or narrower), so line 10's division and line 15's product share one modulo-2^32 domain; the explicit (png_uint_32) cast at line 15 keeps the product in that domain.

png_malloc(png_structp, num_bytes) allocates exactly num_bytes bytes (name-implied standard semantics) or returns NULL under PNG_FLAG_MALLOC_NULL_MEM_OK (set at line 17), so the memset lengths at lines 27-29 and 33 equal the allocated capacity.
png_size_t is at least as wide as png_uint_32, so the length casts in the PNG_1_0_X memset block preserve num_bytes.
limitations: NULL dereference candidate at line 5 (save_flags=p->flags) when png_ptr==NULL: the NULL check at lines 8-9 sits after the dereference and protects nothing on that path, but png_ptr is a parameter with no shown call site, so no NULL producer is demonstrated in the fragment; demoted per the NULL-producer rule.

size == 0 would make the guard at line 10 divide by zero (undefined behavior); no shown statement or call site can produce size == 0 (zlib-style allocators pass per-element sizes >= 1), so it is not a confirmed finding.

Admitted near-boundary values (e.g., items == floor(PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size)) can request allocations up to ~4 GiB; the provenance of items/size is internal and not shown to be attacker-controlled, so this is at most an unconfirmed resource-exhaustion concern, not a memory-safety finding.

verdict.summary: Both shell-execution paths (run_interactively at line 22 and /bin/sh -c via run_program at lines 27-31) are protected: every attacker-influenced field is interpolated inside single-quote delimiters (line 10), and all single quotes are replaced with the literal bytes %27 at lines 12-15 before the command string is built. No value containing a quote-breakout character can reach either sink, so the shell command-injection fix form is present on every path.

utils::replace_all(x, "'", "%27") replaces every occurrence of the single quote in x with the three literal characters %27, matching the shown call syntax.
The single-quote delimiters on line 10 plus the encoded values follow POSIX shell semantics: inside single quotes every character except ' is literal.
The /bin/sh -c argv construction at lines 27-31 confirms that cmdline is parsed as shell syntax, making the sink interpretation explicit.
limitations: Raw CR/LF or other control characters inside the user-supplied fields would still reach the debug LOG write at line 17; demoted because the fragment shows no security-sensitive log consumer or parsing boundary that would make this a log-injection finding.
The return value of run_program (line 31) is passed through to the caller without inspection, but no security decision depends on it.
bookmark_cmd itself comes from the operator's configuration and is trusted; injection-through-configuration is out of scope.

verdict.summary: virgl_cmd_get_capset allocates the caps response with g_malloc (line 14) and initializes only resp->hdr.type (line 15), then transmits sizeof(*resp) + max_size bytes to the guest (line 19). The capset_id/capset_max_version/capset_max_size fields and padding inside *resp are never initialized, disclosing uninitialized host-heap memory to the guest (CWE-908). Additionally, guest-controlled gc.capset_version reaches virgl_renderer_fill_caps (lines 16-18) with no version bound check (the line-10 if (!max_size) guard targets max_size only), and the fill_caps return status is discarded; the OOB write magnitude is library-dependent and is noted as a limitation. The missing one-statement fix is the initialization resp = g_malloc0(sizeof(*resp) + max_size).

evidence.reason: resp is allocated uninitialized at line 14 (resp = g_malloc(sizeof(*resp) + max_size);) and only resp->hdr.type is assigned at line 15, so the capset_id, capset_max_version, capset_max_size fields and padding within sizeof(*resp) hold uninitialized host-heap bytes. The guest entry-point command (VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD at line 7) with a renderer-mapped capset_id passes the line-10 guard (max_size > 0) and reaches this transmit, which sends sizeof(*resp) + max_size bytes to the guest, disclosing uninitialized host memory (CWE-908, use of uninitialized resource). The fix form - initialization via g_malloc0(sizeof(*resp) + max_size) at line 14 - is ABSENT; no zeroing statement appears between allocation and use.

assumptions: struct virtio_gpu_resp_capset layout convention (hdr plus capset_id/capset_max_version/capset_max_size fields followed by capset_data) is established by the shown accesses resp->hdr.type (line 15), resp->capset_data (line 18), and sizeof(*resp) (lines 14, 19).
g_malloc does not zero the returned buffer and aborts on allocation failure (GLib semantics), so resp is never NULL and is uninitialized except for line 15.
VIRTIO_GPU_FILL_CMD(gc) copies the guest-supplied command bytes into gc (entry-point provenance for gc.capset_id and gc.capset_version).
virgl_renderer_get_cap_set returns max_size == 0 for a capset id it cannot map, which is what the line-10 guard rejects.
limitations: Guest-controlled gc.capset_version (residual range 0..UINT32_MAX) reaches virgl_renderer_fill_caps (lines 16-18) with no version bound: if (gc.capset_version > max_ver) is ABSENT and the line-10 if (!max_size) guard is wrong-target drift (constrains max_size, not the version), but the out-of-bounds WRITE magnitude for an out-of-range version depends on unshown callee behavior beyond name-implied semantics, so CWE-787 is not confirmed in-fragment.

The discarded return status of virgl_renderer_fill_caps would amplify the uninitialized-data disclosure (a failed fill leaves the whole data region uninitialized) but is not an independently confirmed finding.
A 32-bit wrap of sizeof(*resp) + max_size in g_malloc is not treated as a finding because max_size is renderer-generated and bounded above 0, not attacker-chosen.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the patched side_in_cb (flatpak dbus-proxy post CVE-fix).
