evidence.reason: Sink is an out-of-bounds write below `char work[BUFFSIZE];` (line 25) whose write cursor starts at `char *workend = &work[sizeof(work) - 2];` (line 32). `prec` originates from an uncapped format-argument read `prec = (long)vto[p->precision].data.num.as_signed;` (line 119, residual range [1, LONG_MAX] after the negative-only guards at lines 122-125 and the default at lines 188-189; reduced only by the digit count at line 198, <= ~22). The only gate before the sink, `if(prec > 0)` (line 205), admits every positive long, so the witness precision 2147483647 (e.g., `%.*d` with value 0, giving zero digits in the loop at lines 193-196) reaches `while(prec-- > 0) *w-- = '0';` (lines 207-208) and writes below `work[0]` for any `prec > sizeof(work)-1` — OOB write CWE-787 with attacker-controlled extent. The absent fix is an upper-bound cap on `prec` before the padding loop (e.g., `if(prec > (long)sizeof(work)) prec = (long)sizeof(work);`); the caps at lines 359-360 and 376-377 guard only the FORMAT_DOUBLE path (line 396) and do not cover this sink.

assumptions: `char work[BUFFSIZE];` (line 25) establishes the object capacity; `workend` (line 32) establishes the in-bounds write span.
A large precision argument (e.g., via `%.*d`) can reach the function, since the fragment itself reads it at line 119 without any cap.

The witness uses `prec = 2147483647` (top of the int precision domain, preserved by the `(long)` cast on LP64), so the out-of-bounds write occurs regardless of the unshown value of the `BUFFSIZE` macro.
limitations: The exact magnitude of the overrun depends on the unshown `BUFFSIZE`; the finding itself holds for any feasible stack-array size because the admitted precision domain is unbounded.
Huge positive field width reaching the OUTCHAR padding loops (e.g., lines 218-219, 237-238) can cause output-loop resource exhaustion — a DoS/robustness concern, not the decisive sink.

FORMAT_DOUBLE: `size_t maxprec` can underflow (lines 369-374) for doubles >= 10^(sizeof(work)-2), and `(sprintf)(work, formatbuf, ...)` (line 396) with a huge double and default precision may exceed `work`; both depend on the unshown `BUFFSIZE` and libc `sprintf` behavior and are not needed for the verdict.
FORMAT_INTPTR writes through `p->data.ptr` (lines 408-417) are `%n`-by-design; any type/size mismatch depends on caller contract not shown here.
`width = -width;` (line 109) on `LONG_MIN` is undefined/robustness-only and not security-decisive for this fragment.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the patched counterpart. Sink W (qemu_chr_fe_write at lines 8-9) is protected by the verbatim equality guard at line 4-6 (if (ibe->outlen == 0) { goto check_reset; }) which excludes the only in-fragment-producible non-positive write length; Sink P (ibe->outpos += ret at line 11) is protected by the verbatim return-status guard at line 10 (if (ret > 0)) which excludes all ret <= 0 values of the write call's return domain, passing the Guard-Identity Audit with no interleaved mutation or type drift; the outbuf[0]/outbuf[1] reset writes have no failure set because the fragment itself indexes outbuf[1] (line 30), implying capacity >= 2. No derivable failing value reaches any dangerous operation.

assumptions: qemu_chr_fe_write has standard write-call semantics: returns a count in [0, len] on success and a negative value on error, so ret > 0 never exceeds the requested length.
outbuf has capacity >= 2 bytes, established by the fragment's own access convention at line 30 (ibe->outbuf[1] = VM_CMD_CHAR;).
The fragment maintains outlen/outpos consistency: both are reset together at lines 19-20 and set to the consistent pair (outlen=2, outpos=0) at lines 31-32.
limitations: An entry state with outpos >= outlen > 0 would make the write length outlen - outpos at line 9 non-positive, but no shown statement in the fragment produces such a state; it is a non-derivable external-state value (Phase 1(c) unconstrained-domain clause).

A chardev that persistently returns 0 or a negative error causes repeated 10 ms timer re-arms (lines 13-16) with no memory-safety impact; this requires environmental chardev behavior not shown in the fragment.

If this fragment were the pre-patch member, the absent one-statement fix would be a return-status check on qemu_chr_fe_write (i.e., if (ret > 0) before ibe->outpos += ret); that statement is present here, which is why the member is judged patched.

verdict.summary: In the base64 branch of hopen_mem, the int return status of hts_decode_base64() at line 16 is discarded. An attacker-controlled malformed payload (e.g. url "data:;base64,AAAA!") passes the guards at lines 6, 10, 12, 14-15, makes the decoder fail without writing *destlen, and leaves `length` (declared uninitialized at line 3) to be consumed at line 26 as the mem-file size against a `size`-byte buffer. The absent one-statement fix is a return-status check on hts_decode_base64() (or an initialization of `length`), preventing uninitialized use (CWE-457) and the resulting out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: `length` is declared uninitialized at line 3 and, on the base64 path, has no writer other than hts_decode_base64() at line 16, whose int status is discarded; on a decoder error for the attacker-controlled payload after `;base64,` (admitted unvalidated at line 12) `*destlen` is not guaranteed to be written, so an uninitialized value is consumed here as the mem-file length for a buffer of capacity `size` from line 13. Guards at lines 15/21 protect only NULL `buffer` and line 27 only NULL `fp` (wrong-target drift for this sink); no `length <= size` check, initialization, or status check exists (all absent fix forms). Uninitialized read consumed by a size/pointer contract -> CWE-457; consequential OOB read on the resulting hFILE_mem.

The return status of hts_decode_base64() is discarded; this call is the sole writer of `length` on this path, and nothing in the fragment detects a failed decode (invalid base64 characters in the unvalidated payload `data = comma+1` from line 7), so an uninitialized `length` propagates to hfile_init_fixed() at line 26 (CWE-457 status-handling chain). The absent fix statement is a return-status check such as `if (hts_decode_base64(buffer, &length, data) < 0) { free(buffer); return NULL; }`.

assumptions: `url` is entry-point/untrusted input (a data: URL supplied to the open path); its suffix after `,` is attacker-controlled and unvalidated by the fragment.
mode must contain 'r' (line 10) for the function to proceed.
malloc(size) with size > 0 succeeds for the witness so that the line 15 NULL check does not preempt the failure path; malloc(0) is avoided by the chosen witness (`strlen("AAAA!") == 5` -> size 3).
hts_decode_base64() is an int-returning decoder whose error path (non-alphabet character) does not guarantee writing *destlen; this is the single callee-contract link in the witness chain.
limitations: The downstream out-of-bounds read occurs inside the hFILE_mem read path after hfile_init_fixed(), which is not shown in the fragment; impact is assessed from the standard fixed-buffer-file semantics.

If hts_decode_percent() can also fail without writing `length`, the percent branch (line 22) has the same latent hazard; no error semantics for it are shown, so it is not a separate confirmed finding.
No decoder out-of-bounds write is confirmed: the shown capacities (lines 13, 19) match standard worst-case decode output, and an overflow depends on unshown callee behavior.
malloc failure on attacker-sized allocations is guarded at lines 15 and 21, so NULL dereference of `buffer` is not a finding in this fragment.

verdict.summary: In FORMAT_DOUBLE, width/precision from the format string and va-list are forwarded into a 32-byte formatbuf with broken length accounting: the precision branch advances fptr by the would-be length of curl_msnprintf (line 367) without the matching `left -= len;` that the width branch has (line 362), so the unguarded appends `*fptr++ = 'f';` and `*fptr = 0;` (lines 377/379) write past `char formatbuf[32]` for long width/precision values admitted by the sign-only guards at lines 358/364. The constructed format is then passed to an unbounded `(sprintf)(work, ...)` (line 383), overflowing `char work[BUFFSIZE]`.

evidence.reason: OOB stack write into `char formatbuf[32]` (line 330). width=1234567890123456789 and prec=9223372036854775807 are admitted by `if(width >= 0)` (line 358) and `if(prec >= 0)` (line 364); line 366's curl_msnprintf returns the would-be length 20, `fptr += len;` (line 367) lands fptr at index 40 (or index 32 under actual-length semantics), and the precision branch lacks the `left -= len;` bookkeeping present at line 362, so this NUL store writes one or more bytes past the 32-byte object — CWE-787.

First unguarded append past `char formatbuf[32]` (line 330): fptr was advanced by the would-be length returned at line 366 (len=20 for prec=9223372036854775807) per standard bounded-printf semantics, reaching index 40; the missing `left -= len;` after line 367 (mirror of line 362) leaves fptr unbounded, so this 'f' store is out of bounds — CWE-787.

Unbounded (sprintf) into `char work[BUFFSIZE];` (line 25): a precision of LONG_MAX (admitted by `if(prec >= 0)` line 364, e.g. format "%.9223372036854775807f") makes formatbuf request ~9.2e18 output digits, overflowing the fixed-size stack array with no size-bounded substitute or precision clamp anywhere on the path — CWE-121.

assumptions: `char formatbuf[32]` (line 330) has capacity 32, valid indices 0..31.
`char work[BUFFSIZE];` (line 25) is a fixed-size stack buffer (any plausible BUFFSIZE value < 9.2e18 suffices for the line-383 overflow).

curl_msnprintf follows standard bounded-sprintf semantics: writes at most `left` bytes and returns the number of characters that would have been written; even under actual-length semantics the line-379 store remains past index 31.

`format`/`ap_save` are entry-point inputs (curl's public printf engine) with no shown bound on width/precision magnitude; the witness widths/precisions are parsed as 64-bit longs per the `(long)` casts at lines 339/345.
`%s` arguments are NUL-terminated C strings, made explicit by the `&& *str` probe at line 285.
limitations: The `p = &vto[param];` sink (line 99) for over-range positional parameters (e.g. `%999999999$d`) is not confirmed: dprintf_Pass1 (line 35) returns nonzero on error and the fragment exits at line 36, but Pass1's internal bounds behavior is not shown, so no witness can be shown to survive that gate; the failing index would need an unshown helper contract.

Width/precision magnitude is only triggerable with 19-digit values inside the format string or parameters; if all callers used small fixed formats the fragment's own reaching values would be small, but no such bound is shown in the fragment.
Huge `width` OUTCHAR loops (lines 140/218/237/246/282/288/317/322) cause output-volume resource consumption only; the memory sink is the caller's buffer and is not a confirmed in-fragment overflow.
Bounds of `f = *end++;` (line 407) depend on unshown dprintf_Pass1 filling of `endpos[MAX_PARAMETERS]` and are not confirmable.

verdict.summary: Every dangerous operation is protected by a shown statement: the heap copy chain at lines 88-90 is covered by the capacity at line 85 (strlen(comment)+strlen(newcomment)+2, sufficient for comment+space+nc+ NUL for all shown-derivable lengths) plus the malloc-NULL guard at line 87; r_core_editor, sdb_decode, r_anal_get_fcn_in, r_meta_get_string, and r_str_between results are NULL-guarded on every use path; the only loop is bounded by i < bb->size; all format strings are literals. No demonstrated failing value reaches any sink; strdup-NULL and getcommapath/caller-contract NULL possibilities are OOM/callee limitations, not confirmed findings.

assumptions: r_meta_get_string returns NULL when no comment exists, and every in-fragment use is guarded (`if (comment && *comment)` line 31, `if (cmtfile && *cmtfile)` line 33, `if (comment)` line 97, `if (!comment || (comment && !strstr(...)))` line 129, `if (comment)` line 155).

r_str_unescape and r_str_ansi_strip are shrink-only transformations of `nc` (each escape consumes >= 2 source chars and emits 1; ANSI stripping removes bytes), so strlen(nc) <= strlen(newcomment) and line 85's Lc+Ln+2 capacity covers the writes at lines 88-90 including the exact-fit no-escape boundary.
r_meta_set_string copies its str argument, so the subsequent free() of nc/text/newcomment at lines 22-27, 92, 102, 132, and 162 is safe.
bb->size spans addresses bb->addr .. bb->addr + bb->size - 1, so i < bb->size (line 59) keeps line 60 in-block.
r_str_newf and r_str_between return NULL only on OOM/no-match; NULL results are passed to NULL-tolerant free()/set_string or guarded.
r_str_trim_head_ro only returns a view at or after the input start of a NUL-terminated string, so strlen(fn)/strlen(newcomment) cannot exceed the original input length.
limitations: strdup(newcomment) (line 80) and strdup(s+1) (line 137) are used without NULL checks (lines 81 and 139); the NULL producer would be malloc OOM on a command-line-sized string, which is not an attacker-demonstrable in-fragment producer, so no CWE-476 finding.
getcommapath(core) result is passed to r_cons_printf without a NULL check (line 36); NULL-producing conditions are not shown.
r_core_editor(core, NULL, comment) (line 71) receives a possibly-NULL comment; its NULL tolerance is an unshown callee contract and no dereference happens in this fragment.
sdb_decode output (line 122) may contain arbitrary bytes, but no security-sensitive consumer of the resulting meta comment is shown.
r_cons_printf of cmtfile (line 36) is a console display print with a literal format, not a log-write or header-construction sink.

Copy-chain safety for the strcat at line 90 relies on the shrink-only semantics of the unshown callees r_str_unescape/r_str_ansi_strip; expansion would be required for an overflow and no shown or standard input produces it.
